reverse_outline.summary: A single payment call conceals four cases that each need a contract with a stated, provider-specific limit, and your own record must cover what falls beyond those limits
Half of the book's recurring incidents at the fictional platform (bad upgrade, dead webhook receiver, rate-limited renewals, double charge) went wrong at the provider's API, not in the money movement
All four incidents share one cause: code treated the payment API as request-and-response when the response was not the whole exchange

An API can pass a slow multi-party payment off as one call only if it gives a contract for each hidden case and states each contract's limit, and since those limits differ by provider you build to your provider's terms and keep your own record for the rest
The five chapters cover the contracts in dependency order, each comparing the two providers' documented terms and marking where public knowledge of their implementation runs out

The API-design chapter argues an integration lasts when it leans on stable identifiers, normalized states and a clear line between immediate and later answers, with the two providers differing on where current state can be read
The idempotency chapter argues a charge is safe to resend only with the same stored, business-derived key sent while the provider still remembers it, which the double-charge incident violated
The versioning chapter argues that pinning each integration to its original version shifts the cost of change rather than removing it, as the one-step jump across three years of changes showed

The webhooks chapter argues a receiver can count only on redelivery within a retry window, so an event is a notice to store and verify against the provider's record, never proof that a payment is unpaid when it is absent

The developer-platform chapter argues that building on an API also needs scoped credentials, a test environment with declared gaps and plannable request limits, since unplanned throttling was misread as payment failure
Readers facing one of the four failures can jump to its chapter, but should otherwise start with API design because every remedy depends on being able to read a payment's identity and state back

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All ten paragraph summaries match the controlling ideas of p01 to p10 in spec order; the KEY POINTS callout matches no spec paragraph and restates the thesis.
The outliner marked no unit as holding two ideas, and none reads as double against its spec entry.
The five chapter paragraphs carry P4-1 to P4-5 one each; the four opening paragraphs set up and state the thesis, and the closing maps the incidents onto the chapters that argue those claims.

Apart from the one failure recorded separately, each evidence item is framed by a sentence saying what it shows: the incidents by 'The four have one cause', the Stripe and Adyen limits by 'The limits are concrete, and they differ', both figures by their captions, and the Double Charge, Version Cliff, Silent Webhook and Renewal Wave by a clause giving the point.

results.quote: Larkfield's payment service has a call named “get payment” that has never asked either provider anything.
results.finding: The Larkfield example ends the paragraph with no sentence saying what it shows (the spec: one name covered a provider's record and Larkfield's memory of it), and the draft omits that the call reads Larkfield's own table. Flow reader B (item B6) did not see why the sentence was there.

All nine declared transitions are expressed at their boundaries: 'The four have one cause' (cause), 'This part's answer is' (problem to solution), 'Five chapters take these contracts in the order' (sequence), 'Each sets ... side by side' into the chapter list (elaboration), 'takes the question that chapter leaves open' (problem to solution), 'a second thing the provider remembers for you' (similarity), 'reverses the direction' (contrast), 'follows from the traffic those four chapters create' (cause), and 'Each of the opening's four shortfalls now has a chapter' (summary).

Both readers describe the same organising principle (incidents, one cause, the part's answer, chapter map in dependency and widening order, entry point), which agrees with the declared flow and its rationale; neither finds any section's position unclear and neither would move a section. The lost-thread points are recorded separately.

results.quote: It must give the developer **a contract for each case the call hides**: an identity and a state for each payment, a key that makes a request safe to repeat, a pinned version, and events for outcomes that arrive after the response.
results.finding: Both readers re-read to pair the four contracts with the four cases of the paragraph before and could not: identity and state answers none of the four cases and the refused request has no contract in the list (nor in Figure 1); the pairing is settled only in 'Where to Begin'. The draft reproduces the spec here: p02 gives four ways including the refusal for volume, p03 promises a contract for each with a list that does not pair, and the spec places the resolving statement in p10.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item B3 (reader A reports it as item A1)

results.quote: The response can be lost, the API can change, the outcome can arrive later, and the request can be refused. The API answers with a readable state, an idempotency key, a pinned version and events.
results.finding: Both readers report that the four cases never appear twice in the same order (callout: lost, changed, later, refused; ¶2: changed, later, refused, lost; closing: lost, changed, missing event, refused) and that they had to match cases to contracts and chapters by hand; in the callout the two lists sit side by side and pair wrongly by position. The callout's order is the draft's own; the difference between ¶2 (incident order) and the closing (chapter order) is declared by the spec in p02 and the callback.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item B2 (reader A reports it as item A2)

results.quote: Sources are cited in each chapter; this introduction makes no factual claim of its own.
results.finding: Both readers stopped here because the sentence reads as contradicting the dated facts about Stripe and Adyen the page has just stated; the intended meaning (every such statement repeats a chapter that cites it) is not what the sentence says. This concerns the wording of the section, not its position, so the waiver does not apply.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item B7 (reader A reports it as item A6)

results.quote: Five chapters take these contracts in the order each depends on the last
results.finding: Reader A counted four contracts against five chapters said to 'take these contracts', and read 'the keys' in the same sentence as idempotency keys until the last chapter paragraph showed they are credentials. Reported by reader A only (item A3).

results.quote: The Version Cliff was one library upgrade that crossed three years of changes in a single step.
results.finding: Reader A re-read this against the opening's 'across a breaking release' (singular) to confirm it is the same incident; 'three years of changes' is new here. Reported by reader A only (item A5).

results.quote: In the Double Charge, Larkfield's job generated a key at each network call
results.finding: The incident names (the Double Charge, The Version Cliff, The Silent Webhook, the Renewal Wave) are used as known proper names in the chapter paragraphs, but the opening tells the four incidents by date and effect without naming them, although the spec's p01 evidence carries the names. Both readers had to go back and match each name to an incident.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A, item A4; flow reader B, item B5

results.quote: the job retried under a new idempotency key
results.finding: 'Idempotency key' is on the audience's does_not_know list and is used in the callout and in the first paragraph before the page glosses it in the third paragraph ('a key that makes a request safe to repeat'). The spec's hook prescribes the term in p01 and places the gloss in p03.
The introduction opens on four dated incidents with figures, reduces them to one cause and states a specific claim; none of the listed weak patterns.
The closing maps the four shortfalls to chapters and gives a course of action; it does not open with a summary formula, add a subtopic, or end on a rephrased thesis alone.

The closing states what no chapter paragraph states (each shortfall has its chapter and all four rest on the first contract, because what can be done depends on what can be read back) and gives the so-what ('If one of them is in front of you, start there'). The 'read in order, the chapters widen' half of the declared synthesis is carried by Figure 2's caption, not by the closing.

'Each of the opening's four shortfalls now has a chapter' returns to the four incidents and matches each way (lost response, changed shape, missing event, refused request) to its chapter, as the callback declares.

The reader of the opening alone predicted the five chapters in roadmap order, the Larkfield and documentation evidence and the tone. The reader of the whole page stated the claim (one call only with a contract for each hidden case and a stated limit for each) and the five chapters' subjects in order, which contains the substance of the expected answer and contradicts none of it.

After the KEY POINTS block the page opens with the four incidents and their ledger figures (6 days; 9 hours and 3,200 memberships; 7,900 renewals; 1,840 members); the opening gives each incident's trigger and effect and leaves the mechanism to the chapter paragraphs and chapters.
